Note that in the following translation the numbers 
without brackets refer to this text, while the numbers in square brackets refer 
to the Greek text. In the English text line numbers short indented lines are 
usually included with the short preceding line (as a single line) in the 
reckoning. Links to explanatory endnotes are indicated by an underlined

(23)
. 
These have been provided by the translator. Stage directions have also been

In this translation, 
possessives of words ending in -s are usually indicated in the common way (that 
is, by adding 
-âs
 (e.g. 
Zeus
 and 
Zeusâs
). This 
convention adds a syllable to the spoken word (the sound 
-iz
). 
Sometimes, for metrical reasons, this English text indicates such possession in 
an alternate manner, with a simple apostrophe. This form of the possessive does

Socrates 
and 

Socratesâ
 are both three-syllable words; whereas, 
Socratesâs
 has 
four syllables).

 (Aris & Phillips, 1985)

BACKGROUND NOTE

 

At the time 
 
Peace 
 
was produced in Athens, the 
city had been at war with Sparta for a number of years. However, peace 
negotiations had been going on, and it looked as if the two sides might just 
agree to end (or at least suspend) their hostilities.

 

PEACE

 

DRAMATIS PERSONAE

 

FIRST SERVANT: a slave belonging to Trygaeus

SECOND SERVANT: a slave belonging to Trygaeus

DAUGHTERS: two daughters of Trygaeus

TRYGAEUS: a middle-aged farmer

HERMES: a god, divine son of Zeus

WAR: a god

UPROAR: a young servant to War.

CHORUS: farmers and servants from different city states

HIEROCLES: a seller of oracles

SICKLE MAKER

JAR MAKER

ARMS DEALER

ARMOURER

TRUMPET MAKER

SPEAR MAKER

BOY, a son of Lamachus

BOY, a son of Cleonymus

PEACE

THEORIA: a young female attendant on Peace

OPORA: a young female attendant on Peace

[Across the back of the flat open space in front of the stage, the Orchestra, are 
four structures: the farm house belonging to Trygaeus, a stable beside or in 
front of it, a cave whose opening is blocked in with rocks, and the palace of 
Zeus. Two of Trygaeusâ slaves are in front of the stable. One is on his knees 
before a shallow tub preparing balls of dung taken from a pile in the yard, and 
the other is carrying these balls of dung into the stable.]

FIRST SERVANT 
 
[coming from the stable door]

Come on, bring us a cake for the beetle.

Get a move on! Hurry up.

 

SECOND SERVANT 
 
[on his knees kneading dung into 
cakes]

                                                    
There you go.

Give him that. May it kill the wretched beast!

I hope he never swallows anything

more delicious than this ball of shit.

 

[First servant takes the cake, goes into the stable, 
and returns.]

 

FIRST SERVANT

Give him another one. And make this cake

out of pounded donkey dung.

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                                       
Back again?

Whereâs the one you took in there just now?

He canât have eaten it.

 

FIRST SERVANT

                                               
Eaten it? By Zeus,

he grabbed it, rolled it round between his feet,                             
10

and then swallowed itâthe whole damn thing.

Hurry up and pound out more, lots of themâ

and pack them tight.

 

[First Servant carries another cake into the stable 
and returns.]

 

SECOND SERVANT 
 
[looking at the audience]

                        
You dung collectors out there, 
 

in the name of the gods, give me a hand,

unless you want to see me choke.                                                          
[10]

 

FIRST SERVANT

                               
Hand me another cakeâ

from a boy prostitute. He says he needs

something made from shit thatâs been well pounded.

 

SECOND SERVANT 
 
[tossing him a cake]

There you go. 

 

[First Servant returns to the stable. The Second 
Servant addresses the audience.]

 

                    
Gentlemen, thereâs one thing

I think Iâll never be found guilty of.

No one will claim that as I
 pound this muck                                  
20

I help myself and eat the stuff.
(1)

 

FIRST SERVANT 
 
[holding his nose]

                                                
Good god!

Get me another, and then bring one more,

and then another. Keep packing more.

 

SECOND SERVANT

No, by Apollo, not me! I canât stand

this disgusting muck a moment longer!

 

FIRST SERVANT

Then Iâll take the dung inside, tub and all.

 

[The First Servant picks up the tub full of dung and 
carries it into the stable.]

 

SECOND SERVANT

To hell with it, by god, and you as well.

 

[Addressing the audience]

 

If any of you knows, please tell me now                                                
[20]

where I can get a nose without a nostril.

Thereâs no work that is more miserable                                        

  30

than rolling this stuff up and serving it

to feed a beetle. Now, a pig or dog,

as soon as someoneâs had a shit, eats it

without a fuss. But this conceited brute,

like some lady, is so full of itself, 
 

it wonât eat unless I mash the stuff all day 
 

then serve it rolled into a ball by hand.

But Iâll take a look, see if itâs done eating.

Iâll open this door, but just a sliver,                                                       
[30]

so it wonât see me.

 

[He pushes the stable door slightly and looks 
inside.]

 

                                    Go onâkeep eating,                                    
40

and donât ever stop, not until you burst

all by yourself in there. That damned creatureâ

look how it eats, mashing with its molars, 
 

moving its head and arms around like that,

like a wrestler or those who twist the cords

to make thick ropes for cargo ships. 
 

 

FIRST SERVANT 
 
[returning from the stable]

                                               
That bruteâ

smelly, foul and greedy! Iâve no idea

what god this stinking apparition comes from,

but I reckon it
 wasnât Aphrodite                                                            
[40]

or the Graces.
(2)

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                
Then who was it? 

 

FIRST SERVANT

                                                         
Itâs got to be                            
 50

some monstrosity sent down here from Zeus, 
 

lord of the thundercrap.

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                                
Well, some youngster

out there in the audience who thinks heâs smart

by this point will be saying, âWhatâs going on?

What does this beetle mean?â And an Ionian 
 

sitting next to him is saying, âIn my view,

itâs a reference to Cleon, showing how

heâs not ashamed to wolf down shit all day.â
(3)

 

FIRST SERVANT 
 
[getting ready to urinate]

Iâm going in to give the beast a drink.

 

[First Servant goes back into the stable.]

 

SECOND SERVANT

Well then, Iâll explain whatâs going on here                                   

60
    
[50]

for children, youngsters, grown ups, and 
 
old men,

even for these self-important windbags.
(4)

My masterâs got some new form of madnessâ

not your kind, but something really new.

All day long he gazes at the heavens

with his mouth open, like this, and cries out,

yelling up at god, âO Zeus,â he says,

âWhat on earth are you doing? Whatâs your plan?

Put that broom aside. Donât sweep Greece away!â

Wait! Hold on! Quiet. I think I hear his voice.                              

  70

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[from inside the house]

O Zeus, what will you do for our people?

Youâll be devastating all our cities

without any sense of what youâre doing.

 

SECOND SERVANT

Thatâs it, the sickness Iâve been talking of.

There you hear a sample of his madness.

When this disturbance first came over him,

heâd keep saying to himself, âHow can I 
 

gain access to Zeus right now?â So he had

some slender ladders made for him, and then,

heâd try to climb them all the way to heaven,                                
 80
    
[70]

until heâd tumble down and break his head.

Well then, damn him, he went out yesterday,

I donât know where, and brought back a beetle,

a monstrous thing from Etna. Heâs forced me

to be its groom, while he keeps stroking it,

as if it were a pony, and saying

âO my little Pegasus, my thoroughbred,

my flying steed, now you must carry me

directly up to Zeus.â Iâll have a look,

bend down here and see just what heâs doing.                              

90

 

[The Second Servant stoops to look through a hole in 
the walls of the stable.]

 

O this is dreadful! Come here, neighbours! Here!

My masterâs rising up into the air,                                                         
[80]

riding astride the beetle like a horse!

 

[Trygaeus appears on the giant dung beetle rising up 
into the air behind the stable.]

 

TRYGAEUS

Easy now, beetle, gently does it, easy.

Donât charge and make things much too rough for me, 
 

trusting your strength, right at the start of things,

not until you sweat, and your beating wings

loosen up your joints and make your muscles free.

I beg you, donât breathe on me that filthy smell.

If you do that, you can stay here in your stall.                              

  100

 

SECOND SERVANT 
 
[calling up to Trygaeus]

Master, my lord, how crazy youâve become!                                          
 [90]

 

TRYGAEUS

Be silent! Hold your tongue!

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                                
Why are you

flapping through the air so senselessly?

 

TRYGAEUS

Iâm soaring off to help out all the Greeks,

a bold new venture, never done before.

 

SECOND SERVANT

Why are you flying? Why this mad sickness?

 

TRYGAEUS

You must speak fair words and never mutter

such trivial sounds. Instead cry out with joy.

Tell men to hold their tongues and to close in

their toilets and their sewers with fresh bricks                              

110
   
[100]

and to plug their arse holes firmly shut.

 

SECOND SERVANT

Thereâs no way Iâll stay quiet, not unless

you tell me where you plan to fly.

 

TRYGAEUS

                                           
Where else, 
 

but up to Zeus in heaven?

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                          
What for?

 

TRYGAEUS

To ask him about each and every Greekâ

what heâs got in store for them.

 

SECOND SERVANT

                                        
And what if

he doesnât tell you?

 

TRYGAEUS

                                                
Iâll take him to
 court

for treason, selling Greeks out to the Medes.
(5)

 

SECOND SERVANT

No, by Dionysus, youâll never go,

not while Iâm alive.

 

TRYGAEUS

                                 
Thereâs no other way.                                  

      120

 

SECOND SERVANT 
 
[shouting into the house]

Help! Help! Help! Children, your fatherâs leavingâ                              
[110]

heâs secretly abandoning you all

to go to heaven. 
 

 

[Trygaeusâs two young daughters come out of the 
house.]

 

                           
You poor wretched girls,

try pleading with your father. Beg him.

 

CHILD

Father, oh father, is this report true,

what those at home are saying about youâ

youâre leaving me here, going up to the sky,

to the birds and the ravens? Youâre trying to fly?
(6)

O daddy, these storiesâare all of them true?

If you love me, I need an answer from you.                                  

   130

 

TRYGAEUS

Yes, my girls, itâs what you think. The truth is

Iâve had it with youâyou keep begging me

for bread and calling me your daddikins,                                              
[120]

when thereâs not a drop of money in the house,

nothing at all. But when Iâm successful,

when I get back again, youâll soon enjoy

a huge cake with my knuckles for a sauce.
(7)

 

DAUGHTER

But how are you going to finish the trip?

You canât travel that road in a sailing ship.

 

TRYGAEUS

I won't be sailing on the sea in a ship.                              

             
140

I'll be flying up there on a horse with wings.

 

DAUGHTER

Daddy, how did you plan to capture this thing,

harness it, and go to the gods on the wing?

 

TRYGAEUS

In those stories by Aesop, I found out

the beetle was the only beast with wings                                              
[130]

that could reach the place where gods reside.

 

DAUGHTER

Father, father, thatâs false. All folks deny

stories which say that stinking brutes fly

and can rise to the gods way 
on high.

 

TRYGAEUS

                                    
Once, long ago,

when it had a quarrel with an eagle,                                              

150

it went up there and took out its revenge

by rolling from the nest the eagleâs eggs.

 

DAUGHTER

Why not hitch Pegasus and his divine wings?

The gods would receive you as our tragic king.

 

TRYGAEUS

My dear girl, Iâd have needed twice the food.

But now whatever meal I eat myself

will serve to feed this beetle, too.

 

DAUGHTER

But what if it falls in the depths out at sea?                                          
[140]

With wings like those ones, how will it flee?

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[lifting up his phallus or exposing his 
penis]

For that Iâve got this rudder I can use.                                         
 
 160

And the beetle will be
 just like those boats

they make in Naxos.
(8)

 

DAUGHTER

                                             
But then as you float,

what harbour will open to welcome that boat?

 

TRYGAEUS

Doesnât Piraeus have a Beetle Harbour?
(9)

 

DAUGHTER

Beware of collisions. You might fall down

from way up there and become a lame clown.

If so, for Euripides youâll be a 
 
story--

heâll turn you into a tragical glory.
(10)

 

TRYGAEUS

Iâll watch out for that. And now good bye!

 

[Trygaeus addresses the audience as he starts moving 
higher.]

 

 And you for whom Iâm doing all this work,                                   
170      
150

for the next three days you must not fart or crap.

If this creature smells that while in the air,

itâll toss me head first and come down to graze.

So come now, Pegasus, be off. Good luck.

Keep those bright ears of yours pricked up

and shake that golden bridle and your bit

until they rattle. What are you doing?

What are you up to? Why turn your nose

toward those stinking sewers? Let yourself

go bravely up above the earth, stretch out                                    

180     [160]

those racing wings of yours and head straight for

the halls of Zeus. Keep your nose out of the shit,

away from all the food you eat each day.

Hey, that man down there, what are you doing?

I mean that one crapping in Piraeus,

right by the whorehouse. Youâre destroying me,

doing me in. Canât you please bury the stuff,

pile lots of earth on top, and then plant thyme

and pour perfume on it? If I fell down

and something happened to me from up here                               
190

and killed me, the state of Chios would 
 
be fined                                  
[170]

five talents, all because of your ass hole.
(11)

O my god, Iâm scared. And Iâm not joking,

not any more. You there working this machine,

take good care of me. Right now thereâs a wind

twisting its way around my belly button. 
 

If you donât watch it, Iâll be making stuff

to feed the beetle. But it seems to me

Iâm getting near the gods. Yes, I can see

the home of Zeus.

 

[By this point the beetle has descended and come to 
rest in front of the house of Zeus. Trygaeus gets off the beetle and knocks on 
the door.]

 

                  
Whoâs in there, in Zeusâ house?                                    
200

Why wonât you open up?

 

HERMES 
 
[from inside]

                                                   
A human voice!                                    
[180]

Where did that come from?

 

[Hermes opens the door and sees Trygaeus and the dung 
beetle.]

 

                                                    
Lord Hercules!

Whatâs that disgusting thing?

 

TRYGAEUS

                                                
A horse beetle.

 

HERMES

You disgusting, reckless, shameless creature!

You scoundrel, you consummate rascal,

the worst rogue there is! How did you get here,

you most villainous of all the villains?

Whatâs your name? Speak up, wonât you?

 

TRYGAEUS

Super-scoundrel.

 

HERMES

                            
In what country were you born?

Tell me.

 

TRYGAEUS

                    
Super-scoundrel.

 

HERMES

                                                 
Whoâs your father?                      

       210

 

TRYGAEUS

My father? Super-scoundrel.

 

HERMES

                                                       
By this earth,

youâll die for sure if you donât give your name. 
 

 

TRYGAEUS

Iâm Trygaeus and Iâm 
 
from Athmonum,

a good vine-grower.
(12)
 
I donât slander people,                                      
[190]

and I donât like disputes.

 

HERMES

                                          
Why have you come?

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[handing Hermes a steak]

To offer you this meat.

 

HERMES 
 
[grabbing the meat and in a very different 
tone]

                                         
You poor fellow,

how did you get here?

 

TRYGAEUS

                                
Well, sticky fingers,

you see how you no longer think of me

as the vilest of all rogues. Please be off now

and summon Zeus for me.

 

HERMES

                                                  
O dear, dear, dear!                   
         220

You wonât reach the gods. Youâre not even close.

Theyâve gone away. They moved out yesterday.

 

TRYGAEUS

Where on earth did they go?

 

HERMES

                                       
They wouldnât go to earth!

 

TRYGAEUS 

Well, then, where?

 

HERMES

                         
Oh, a long, long way away,

under the very dome of heaven itself.

 

TRYGAEUS

So why have you been left here by yourself?                                        

 [200]

 

HERMES

Iâm keeping an eye on the furniture,

whatâs left of itâsome little pots and pans,

boards, some wine jugs.

 

TRYGAEUS

                             
Why have the gods all left?

 

HERMES

Theyâre angry at the Greeksâso they moved War                       

  230

into the house where they were living
,

giving him full power to treat you Greeks

any way he wishes. They moved their home

even higher up, as far as they could go,

so they wouldnât see you fighting any more

or hear any of your prayers.

 

TRYGAEUS

                                                        
Tell me thisâ

why have they been treating us like that?                                             
[210]

 

HERMES

Because they tried to make peace many times,

but you prefer to fight. If the Spartans

had a small success, theyâd say something
 like,                             
240

âBy the twin gods, those Attic types will pay.â
(13)

And if, with events turning out quite well

for those in Attica, the Spartans came

to talk of peace, youâd answer right away,

âBy Athena, theyâre playing tricks with us.

No, by Zeus, thereâs no way weâll go along.

Theyâll come back, if we hang on to Pylos.â
(14)

 

TRYGAEUS

Yes, thatâs way folks in our country 
talk.                                               
[220]

 

HERMES

Well, thatâs why I donât think youâll ever see

Peace in your time again.

 

TRYGAEUS

                                  
Whereâs she gone, then?                             

     250

 

HERMES

War has thrown her into a deep hole. 

 

TRYGAEUS

                                                      
What hole?

 

HERMES 
 
[pointing to the walled up cave in the central 
part of the stage.]

 

That one, way down there. Whatâs more,

you see how many rocks heâs piled on top

to stop you hauling her back out again.

 

TRYGAEUS

Tell me, whatâs War planning to do to us?

 

HERMES

All I know is last evening he brought home

a gigantic mortar.

 

TRYGAEUS

                               
Heâs got a mortar?                                                    
[230]

Whatâs he going to do with that?

 

HERMES

                                    
Well, he wants it

to pulverize the city states of Greece.

But I have to go. I think heâs coming outâ                                   

 260

heâs making such a fuss in there.

 

[Hermes leaves. The noise inside the house gets 
louder.]

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[alarmed]

                                                      
Oh, oh!

Iâm in a mess. Come on, Iâd better find

some way to get away from him. I think

I hear the sounds of a warlike mortar.

 

[Trygaeus conceals himself. War enters, carrying a 
huge mortar and a basket of vegetables.]

 

WAR

O you human
 

beings, you mortal men,

you human creatures who endure so much,

how your jaws are going to feel the pain!

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[from his hiding place]

By lord Apollo, look at the mortar,

the size of it! This is a disasterâ

that look heâs got! Is this the enemy                                             
 
270
   
[240]

weâre running fromâso 
 
terrible, so tough,

so hard on a manâs legs?
(15)

 

WAR 
 
[taking some leeks and putting them in the 
mortar]

                                                                                     
O Prasiae!

thrice damned, five times damned, damned a
 thousandfold!

This very day youâre going to be demolished.
(16)

 

TRYGAEUS

This is no concern of ours, gentlemen,

since itâs a problem for the Spartans.

 

WAR 
 
[putting some garlic in the mortar]

O Megara, Megara, how very soon

you be crushed to bits, turned into mincemeat.
(17)

 

TRYGAEUS

Whoa, my goodness me, heâs throwing in

some bitter tears for the Megarians,                                              

280

big ones, too.

 

WAR 
 
[grating some cheese into the mortar]

               And Sicily, youâre destroyed, as well.                                       
[250]

 

TRYGAEUS

Such a great state to be grated down

in such a miserable way.

 

WAR 
 
[pouring honey over the food]

                                                 
All right, 
 

lets pour over this some Attic honey.

 

TRYGAEUS

Hey, Iâd advise you use a different honey.

That stuff costs four obols. So ease up

with that stuff from Attica.

 

WAR 
 
[calling for his servant] 
 

                                
Boy! Boy! Uproar!

 

[Uproar enters from the house.]

 

UPROAR

Whyâd you call me?

 

WAR

                                                    
Iâll make you really yelp!

Standing there doing nothing. Hereâs a fist for you!

 

[War punches Uproar in the face.]

 

UPROAR

That hurts! O master, Iâm in agony!                                            
     290

Your fist wasnât full of garlic, was it?

 

WAR

Why donât you run and fetch me a pestle?

 

UPROAR

We donât have one. It was only yesterday                                              
[260]

when we moved in here.

 

WAR

                                     
Then go get one

from the Atheniansâand make it fast.

 

UPROAR

By god, Iâll do it. If I donât find one,

then Iâll be beaten till I howl.

 

[Uproar runs off in a hurry.]

 

TRYGAEUS

                                                   
Well now,

what are we poor wretched types to do?

You see thereâs great danger threatening us.

If he returns and brings along a pestle,                                          
300

War will sit there using it to pulverize

all our city states. O Dionysus, 
 

may he perish and not get back with it!

 

[Uproar comes running back empty handed.]

 

WAR

Here he is.

 

UPROAR

                      
Whatâs going on?

 

WAR

                                                     
You didnât bring it?  

 

UPROAR

The strange thing is thisâthose Athenians

have lost their pestle, 
 
that tanner who ground                                     
[270]

all Greece to powder.
(18)

 

TRYGAEUS

                                               
By Athena,

that sovereign lady, he did well to die,

just when the city needed him to go,

before he dumped us all into that hash.                                        
  310

 

WAR

Then go get another one in Sparta

and be quick about it.

 

UPROAR

                                
Iâm off master.

 

[Uproar moves off quickly. War shouts after him.]

 

WAR

And get back here on the double.

 

TRYGAEUS 
 
[to the audience]

                                                          
Well, men,

whatâs going to happen to us? At this point,

weâre in deep trouble. So if one of you,

by chance, is an initiate of Samothrace,

this would be a splendid time for you
 to pray

the servant lad sprains both his feet.
(19)

 

UPROAR 
 
[running back on stage and striking an 
exaggerated pose]

                                                            
Alas!                                             

[280]

O woe is me! And one more time Alas! 
 

 

WAR
